blocks.content: Mountains are an important physical feature of India. They influence the country's climate, drainage system, vegetation and human activities. The major mountain systems of India include the Himalayan Mountains and the Peninsular Mountains. These mountains also play an important role in protecting India from cold winds, influencing monsoon rainfall, and serving as the source of many important rivers.
1. Himalayan Mountain System

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Himalayan Mountain System consists of three parallel ranges: Greater Himalayas (Himadri), Lesser Himalayas (Himachal), and Outer Himalayas (Shiwaliks).
Trans-Himalayan ranges include the Karakoram, Ladakh, and Zaskar ranges, housing major glaciers like Siachen and Baltoro.
Peninsular India features diverse mountain systems including the ancient fold mountains of the Aravallis, block mountains of Vindhyas and Satpuras, and coastal ghats.
The Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats converge at the Nilgiri Hills, with Doddabetta as its prominent peak.
Indian mountains serve as crucial climatic barriers, sources of major perennial rivers, and global biodiversity hotspots.

blocks.content: The Himalayas are the youngest fold mountains in the world. They extend for about 2400 km from Jammu & Kashmir in the west to Arunachal Pradesh in the east. The Himalayas were formed due to the collision between the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate.
2. Major Himalayan Peaks
3. Trans-Himalayan Ranges
• Karakoram Range – Contains K2, the second highest peak in the world.
• Ladakh Range – Located north of the Great Himalayas.
The Himalayas act as a natural climatic barrier protecting the Indian subcontinent from cold Central Asian winds and directing monsoon rains.
• Zaskar Range – Located between Ladakh and Himachal.
4. Peninsular Mountain System
The Peninsular mountains are older than the Himalayas. They are mainly formed of hard igneous and metamorphic rocks. These mountains are more stable and have experienced less tectonic activity.

cells: Run parallel to western coast; average height about 900–1600 m

blocks.content: 5. Western Ghats vs Eastern Ghats

rows: Continuous range, crossed through passes (Thal, Bhor, Pal Ghats)
Discontinuous and eroded by east-flowing rivers
Heavy orographic rainfall on the western slopes
Receives rain mainly during retreating NE monsoons
Source of major peninsular rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri)
No major rivers originate from these ghats

blocks.content: 6. Importance of Mountains in India
• Mountains act as natural barriers and protect the country.
• They influence the climate and monsoon rainfall.
• They are the source of major rivers.
• They provide forests, biodiversity and natural resources.
• They support tourism and hill stations.

items: Aravalli Range is the oldest fold mountain system in India; its highest peak is Guru Shikhar (1,722 m) in Mount Abu.
Anamudi (2,695 m) in the Anaimalai Hills is the highest peak of Peninsular India as well as the Western Ghats.
Western Ghats are continuous and can be crossed only through key passes: Thal Ghat, Bhor Ghat, and Pal Ghat.
K2 (Godwin-Austen) at 8,611 m is located in the Trans-Himalayan Karakoram Range.

blocks.content: Important Facts
• The Himalayas are the youngest fold mountains.
• Kanchenjunga is the highest peak in India.
• Aravalli Range is among the oldest mountain systems.
• Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage biodiversity hotspot.
